The door clicks shut behind you. Minus eighteen degrees, no phone signal, and nobody due back for hours.
A walk-in freezer holds meat solid for months, and it will start doing the same to your fingers within about thirty minutes.
First, find the release, since by law every modern walk-in has a knob inside that opens the door even when it is padlocked.
While you search, remember the real enemy is not the cold itself but the fan, which strips heat off your skin like wind.
Get out of the airflow, behind a stack of boxes, and get up off the floor, because that floor is the coldest surface in the room.
Build a nest, cardboard beneath you, cardboard around you, and cling film over your clothes to trap warm air.
Keep your hands in your armpits and your head covered, because fingers, ears and nose freeze long before anything else.
Do not pace to stay warm, sweat soaks your clothes, and wet cloth loses heat twenty five times faster than dry.
Make noise on a schedule, a pan against the door every few minutes, because sound travels through steel far better than a phone signal.
Dressed for a kitchen you have hours, not minutes, and shivering is simply your body working, so let it.
Here is the twist, the inside release is usually buried behind stacked boxes or frost, so clear it before you panic.
So tell someone before you go in, and prop the door open, because the coldest place in the building is the one everyone forgot.
